In the core tutorials (T1–T9), the measles model ran as compartments: the numbers of people in S, E, I, and R. This tutorial runs it as **agents**: each person has their own state, their own times of moving between states, and, if you want, their own infectiousness and susceptibility. The model is written as before; what changes is what you can ask of it.

By the end of this tutorial, you'll understand how to:

- run a disease as agents, and change the parameters of a built-in disease;
- look at the state and history of each person;
- see how chance decides whether one imported case starts an outbreak;
- give people different infectiousness, so that a few cause most infections (superspreading);
- let immunity wane, and count how many times each person is infected.

## Step 1: A disease as agents

Here is the SEIR measles model from [T3](t3_disease.qmd). Giving the sim `n_agents=` instead of `total_pop=` runs it as agents (as does `solver='abm'`), here 5,000 people:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))

sims = {
    'Compartments (ODE)': ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=5000, stop=ss.days(150)),
    'Agents':             ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(150)),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

The two agree closely. They differ a little because agents take whole daily steps (the run prints a note on this) and each agent's course is random. Everything in the core tutorials works the same way for agents.

Starsim also has ready-made diseases, customized with parameters. Here is the built-in `ss.SIR`, with parameters close to measles:

```{python}
sir = ss.SIR(dur_inf=ss.days(8), beta=ss.perday(1.9), init_prev=0.001, p_death=0.002)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(60))
sim.run()
sim.plot()
```

Here `dur_inf` is the mean infectious period, `beta` the transmission rate, `init_prev` the share infected at the start, and `p_death` the share of infected people who die. The results are in `sim.results.sir`. `ss.SIR`, `ss.SIS`, and `ss.SEIR` are the textbook models, with exponential durations. The Starsim library (`import starsim.library as ssl`) has fuller models of about twenty diseases, such as `ssl.Measles`, `ssl.Influenza`, and `ssl.TB`, used in the same way, e.g. `ss.Sim(ssl.Measles(), networks=ss.RandomNet(), n_agents=5000)`; see the [Diseases page of the model library](../user_guide/library_diseases.qmd).

## Step 2: Looking at individual people

As agents, the sim keeps each person's state, and when they entered it and are due to leave it. `sim.people.to_df()` gives a row per person (`measles.ti_E` is the step each was infected, `measles.ti_I` the step they became infectious):

```{python}
sim = sims['Agents']
df = sim.people.to_df()
df.loc[:, ['uid', 'age', 'female', 'measles.S', 'measles.R', 'measles.ti_E', 'measles.ti_I']].head()
```

`sim.people.get_person(uid)` gives everything about one person, and a state gives the IDs (UIDs) of the people in it: `measles.R.uids` are those who have recovered. In [T3](t3_disease.qmd), an Erlang latent period changed the epidemic, compared with an exponential one of the same mean; as agents, you can see why, since each person draws their own:

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
progression = E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=10, mean=ss.days(10)) # Latent for 10 days on average, with less spread
measles_erlang = ss.Disease(S >> E @ 1.9*I, progression, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')
sim_erlang = ss.Sim(measles_erlang, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
sim_erlang.run()

plt.figure()
for label, s in {'Exponential': sim, 'Erlang (k = 10)': sim_erlang}.items():
    latent = s.diseases.measles.E.stays # How long each person who has been through E stayed there: their latent period, in days
    print(f'{label}: mean latent period {np.mean(latent):.1f} days')
    plt.hist(latent, bins=np.arange(0, 40), alpha=0.5, label=label)
plt.xlabel('Latent period (days)')
plt.ylabel('Number of people')
plt.legend();
```

With an exponential latent period, short ones are the most common, and many take three weeks or more; with an Erlang distribution, most people become infectious 6 to 17 days after infection. Both average about 10 days, in whole days since agents move in whole steps. `E.stays` covers everyone who has entered and left E. (Subtracting `m.ti_I - m.ti_E` would give a day more, since an infection happens at the end of its step and becoming infectious at the start of one.) [Array indexing](../user_guide/mechanics_indexing.qmd) shows other ways to pick out people, and [People and agents](../user_guide/populations_people.qmd) what each person has.

## Step 3: Chance, and the first case

In a compartmental model, an infection with R above 1 always takes off. In reality, the first cases may recover before infecting anyone, and the outbreak dies out by chance. Agents capture this.

Take the town of [T5](t5_interventions.qmd), where 90% of people are immune, and suppose one infectious person arrives. Each case then infects about 1.9 × 8 × 0.1 ≈ 1.5 others. Here are 20 runs as agents, each with its own random seed and line (`lines=True`), and the ODE for comparison:

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1)) # 90% immune, and 1 case

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(ss.Sim(measles, **pars), n_runs=20)
msim.plot('measles.I', lines=True)

ode = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=5000, stop=ss.days(365), solver='ode', verbose=0)
ode.run()
ode.plot('measles.I')
```

The ODE always gives the same outbreak. As agents, some runs give one about as large, and the rest die out after a handful of cases. Counting runs with fewer than 20 infections:

```{python}
total = msim.results.measles.infection.values.sum(axis=1) # Total infections in each run
print('Share of introductions that die out:', np.mean(total < 20))
```

Theory says one case dies out with a chance of 1/R (for an exponential infectious period), here about 2 in 3, close to the runs. This matters for questions about introductions: how likely an imported case is to start an outbreak, or how long a place stays free of a disease.

## Step 4: People who differ: superspreading

For many diseases, most cases infect few others or none, and a few infect many (superspreading). This is usually described by giving each person an infectiousness drawn from a gamma distribution with mean 1 and shape (dispersion) k: the smaller k, the more transmission is concentrated (SARS in 2003 had k near 0.16).

A value that each person has is an attribute, `ss.attr()`: here, drawn once for each person when they are made (a trait). `ss.modify()` then multiplies each person's infectiousness (`rel_trans`) by it:

```{python}
def make_sim(k=None):
    """ The measles model, with the infectiousness of each person drawn from a gamma distribution with shape k """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    if k is None: # Everyone equally infectious
        measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1))
        return ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
    infectiousness = ss.attr(ss.gamma(shape=k, scale=1/k)) # A mean of 1, and a shape (dispersion) of k
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, infectiousness=infectiousness, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1))
    superspreading = ss.modify(measles.rel_trans, multiply=infectiousness)
    return ss.Sim(measles, connectors=superspreading, **pars)

for label, k in {'Everyone equally infectious': None, 'k = 1': 1, 'k = 0.2': 0.2}.items():
    msim = ss.parallel(make_sim(k), n_runs=40)
    total = msim.results.measles.infection.values.sum(axis=1)
    print(label, '- share that die out:', np.mean(total < 20), '- median size of the outbreaks that take off:', np.median(total[total >= 20]))
```

Each case infects about 1.5 others on average in all three, but the more concentrated transmission is, the more often an introduction dies out: with k = 0.2, about 4 in 5 do, since the first case is most likely one who infects nobody. The outbreaks that take off are of similar size, but can start explosively, from a single event. A compartmental model can't show this, having no individuals to differ.

`ss.attr()` can also draw a value when something happens to a person (e.g. a severity at infection, with `when=infection`), or record one; see [Diseases](../user_guide/building_diseases.qmd). Susceptibility can differ in the same way, with `ss.modify(measles.rel_sus, ...)`.

## Step 5: Immunity that wanes

Measles leaves lifelong immunity, but many infections don't. In an SIRS model, recovered people become susceptible again, letting a disease become endemic rather than burning out. It takes one more transition, from R to S. Here it is for a generic respiratory infection (R0 = 0.4 × 7 = 2.8) with immunity lasting 6 months on average, compared with no waning:

```{python}
def make_cold(waning):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I        # β = 0.4 per day
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(7)   # Infectious for 7 days on average
    infections = ss.attr(1, when=infection, combine='sum', init=0) # The number of times each person has been infected
    transitions = dict(infection=infection, recovery=recovery)
    if waning:
        transitions['waning'] = R >> S @ ss.days(180) # Immune for 6 months on average
    return ss.Disease(**transitions, infections=infections, init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

pars_cold = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(3*365), verbose=0)
sims = {
    'SIR (lasting immunity)': ss.Sim(make_cold(waning=False), **pars_cold),
    'SIRS (immunity wanes)':  ss.Sim(make_cold(waning=True), **pars_cold),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')
```

With lasting immunity, there is one epidemic. When immunity wanes, susceptible people are replenished, and the infection returns in waves that settle at an endemic level.

The attribute `infections` counts each person's infections (`combine='sum'` adds 1 at each): a history, which only agents have. An analyzer that adds 1 for each person infected in each step (`cold.infection.uids`) gives exactly the same counts. After three years with waning immunity:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
counts = sims['SIRS (immunity wanes)'].people.cold.infections.values
plt.figure()
plt.hist(counts, bins=np.arange(counts.max() + 2) - 0.5)
plt.xlabel('Number of infections in 3 years')
plt.ylabel('Number of people');
```

## Explicit

```{python}
class CountInfections(ss.Analyzer):
    """ The number of times each person has been infected, counted by hand """
    def init_post(self):
        super().init_post()
        self.counts = np.zeros(len(self.sim.people), dtype=int)
        self.counts[self.sim.diseases.cold.I.uids] = 1 # The people infectious at the start
    def step(self):
        self.counts[self.sim.diseases.cold.infection.uids] += 1 # The people infected in this step

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
cold = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.4*I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(7), waning=R >> S @ ss.days(180), init_prev=0.01) # No attribute
counted = ss.Sim(cold, analyzers=CountInfections(), **pars_cold)
counted.run()

counts = counted.analyzers.countinfections.counts
plt.figure()
plt.hist(counts, bins=np.arange(counts.max() + 2) - 0.5)
plt.xlabel('Number of infections in 3 years')
plt.ylabel('Number of people');
```
:::

Everyone is infected at least once, most people 3 to 5 times, varying by chance. A model can use a person's history: e.g. `ss.modify(cold.rel_sus, multiply=0.5, who=cold.infection.n_times >= 2)` would halve the susceptibility of people infected at least twice.

## Writing a disease as code

Every disease above is declared, as states and transitions. A disease can also be written as Python code: a class whose methods say what happens to each agent at each step, as in Starsim 3. This suits a course easier to say in code than in transitions (e.g. a CD4 count that falls continuously); [A5](a5_modules.qmd) shows how. Several interacting diseases are in [T8](t8_strata.qmd).

## Exercises

1. **Parameter exploration**: Try different durations of immunity in the SIRS model (e.g. 1, 6, and 24 months). How do they affect the epidemic curve, and the number of times people are infected?
2. **SEIRS model**: Add a latent period of 2 days to the SIRS model, to make an SEIRS model. Does it change the endemic level?
3. **Superspreading and control**: In the town with 90% immune, increase the share susceptible to 20% (`init=dict(R=0.8)`), so that each case infects about 3 others. What share of introductions die out now, with and without superspreading (k = 0.2)?

## Further reading

- [Covasim: getting started](https://docs.covasim.org/tutorials/tut_intro.html): an agent-based model of COVID-19, built on similar ideas
- [Superspreading and the effect of individual variation on disease emergence](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04153): the paper that introduced the dispersion k
- [EpiModel: introduction](https://epimodel.github.io/EpiModel/articles/Intro.html): deterministic, individual contact, and network versions of the classic models, in R
